topics/lti-representation-conversions.ht.title: Converting LTI System Representations
topics/lti-representation-conversions.ht.description:
The LTI state-space representation has a state equation, which describes the system dynamics,and an output equation, which produces the outputs of interest:LTI systems can be represented by block diagrams, transfer functions, ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and state space.Figure Routes between LTI system representations. ODE to transfer function: take the Laplace transform; reverse the conversion with the inverse Laplace transform. ODE to state space: use one state equation for each phase variable; reverse the conversion by combining state equations algebraically. ODE to block diagram: use one integrator per phase variable; reverse the conversion by manipulating the diagram into phase variables in an integrator chain. State space to transfer function: use the system transfer operator. To go from a transfer function to state space, use another form first. State space to block diagram: use one integrator per state equation; reverse the conversion with one state equation per integrator. Transfer function to block diagram: build a chain of integrators; reverse the conversion with block-diagram algebra, including . Starting with the state equation, take the Laplace transform:The dimensions of areThis produces a transfer function for each input/state-output combination:Take the Laplace transform of the output equation and substitute the state relation:The system transfer operator relates each of the inputs to each of the outputs.To invert , use its determinant and adjugate:Thus,Very often, is the zero matrix.Use one integrator for each state variable. The output of each integrator is that state variable.For example,
Figure A two-state realization with one integrator per state variable. For a single output: Differentiate the output equation as many times as needed to match the system order: times. Differentiate the state equations as many times as needed to match the system order: times. Substitute the state equations, differentiated state equations, and output equations into the differentiated output equations until the state variables are eliminated. Depending on the system, this can be a lot of work or very simple. Derivatives of inputs are likely to appear.Use block-diagram algebra to form feedback loops, then collapse the loops using
Figure Negative-feedback loop reduction. Use block-diagram algebra to form an integrator chain leading to .
Figure Rearranging the diagram into an integrator chain. Select each state variable as the output of an integrator.
Figure Choosing states at integrator outputs. Distribute the transfer function and divide through by to obtain integrators instead of differentiators. Manipulate the result as desired.For example,The term indicates that the system responds to .
Figure An integrator realization of the transfer function. We can stop here or aim for an integrator chain.Swap the integrator and summing junction. Move the summing-junction port to the left, introducing the indicated block on the gain-2 input path. Move the feedback pickoff point to the left, introducing an block in the gain-4 feedback path. Combining the summing junctions gives an input section and an integrator-chain section.
Figure Rearranging the realization into an integrator chain. Swap the two halves of the diagram, then move the output pickoff point to the left across the last integrator. The block is eliminated.The resulting direct form has: No derivatives. Minimal integrators. An integrator chain.
Figure Completing the direct-form realization. Distribute the transfer function and take the inverse Laplace transform:There is no good process for this conversion directly. Convert to an ODE or block diagram first, then convert to state space.Use the ODE to build an integrator chain:
Figure Building and reducing an integrator-chain diagram from an ODE. topics/normal-trees.html.title: Normal Trees
topics/normal-trees.html.description: A subgraph is a subset of the nodes and branches of another graph.A spanning subgraph includes all nodes from the original graph and a subset of its branches.A tree is a graph with no loops. There is a unique path to each node.A spanning tree is a subgraph with all original nodes and no loops.A normal tree is a spanning tree built from a linear graph. Branches that are removed are called links. Remaining branches are called twigs.The selection of which branches to remove assigns causality. The goal is to maximize system order.Links are branches removed from the normal tree. Their primary variable, on the left-hand side of the elemental equation, is the through variable. Their secondary variable, on the right-hand side, is the across variable.Twigs are branches in the normal tree. Their primary variable is the across variable, and their secondary variable is the through variable.The system order isTherefore,For example: A mass is an IESE if it is a twig because its primary variable is the energy storage variable, . An inductor is an IESE if it is a link. The following steps convert a linear graph into a normal tree using a subtractive approach. The book uses an additive approach that also works.Step 0. Start with a copy of a correct linear graph, or work on top of the graph.Step 1. Remove all T-type sources. If the tree is now non-spanning, then the linear graph is wrong.Step 2. Remove as many T-type elements as possible such that the tree is still spanning.Step 3. If needed, remove as many D-type elements as possible such that the tree is still spanning.Step 4. If still needed, remove the minimal number of A-type elements until no loops remain.Step 5. If loops remain due to A-type sources, the linear graph is wrong.A force acts to the right on a mass . A damper and spring connect the mass in series to a fixed wall. The mass velocity is , and the velocity of the damper–spring junction is .For , both the damper and spring are in compression.Figure Mechanical system, linear graph, and annotated normal tree. The system has orderwith as an A-type twig and as a T-type link.

Differential equations involve:
One or more dependent variables (unknowns) and their derivatives.
One or more independent variables (knowns), together with inputs or forcing functions.
The goal is to solve for the dependent variables in terms of the independent variables.Historical ME322 coverage excludes partial differential equations (PDEs) and focuses on ordinary differential equations (ODEs). ODEs have only one independent variable.The most general ODE with one dependent variable isHere, is some function of the dependent variable , its derivatives, and the independent variable . The ODE is of order .The most general linear ODE isIt consists only of linear combinations of the dependent variable and its derivatives, together with a forcing function such as .The terms are coefficients:
Functions of time for a time-varying system.
Constants for a time-invariant system.
The input or forcing function is . If , the ODE is homogeneous.Lumped-parameter linear time-invariant (LTI) systems lead to linear ODEs with constant coefficients. These can be solved using the Laplace transform, the method of undetermined coefficients, and other techniques.ConsiderLet be any function satisfying the nonhomogeneous ODE. This is the particular solution.Let be the solution to the homogeneous ODE. Depending on the order, this complementary solution may have multiple terms:This assumes that solves the ODE. Wait until then to find and .Chooseto match the forcing function . Form the complementary solution (see Section 8.3.1): Find using the method of undetermined coefficients (see Section 8.3.2). Annotated lecture rendition.Brushes provide rotational contact between the rotor and stator to conduct current across the rotating boundary. Along with the commutator, they provide: Electrical commutation, or switching of current, to provide DC torque output. Rectification of back-EMF to provide DC output voltage.
Figure Commutation rectifies the alternating profile. The back-EMF and torque profiles, defined by the dynamic coefficientare alternating waveforms rather than constant. Consequently, for constant current the torque output is sinusoidal, and for constant velocity the back-EMF is sinusoidal. The model so far is a PMAC motor model rather than a PMDC motor model.Commutation is needed to rectify these waveforms. As the brushes pass along commutator segments, the constant input current alternates in phase with the torque profile, always producing positive torque. Commutation also makes the output voltage, or motor back-EMF, always positive.
Figure Current paths through a multiphase winding. Current enters the positive brush and splits between commutator segments 1 and 7. Half goes clockwise from , and the other half goes counterclockwise from . The resultant is always close to horizontal and therefore perpendicular to , maximizing torque output.
